We evaluate when the extra precision matters. In the synthetic mixtures, most of the gain in predicting the realized cosine comes from normalizing each component before averaging. The low-dimensional experiments show where Taylor errors can persist even after adding many coordinates of negligible variance (Section~\ref{sec:synth}). The posterior experiments show larger discrepancies among estimators of the cosine variance (Section~\ref{sec:unc}). On incomplete real data, estimates based on the same fitted law have similar prediction errors when they use the angular moments or their stronger approximations (Section~\ref{sec:missing}).

We then ask when the additional precision changes the results. A simple bound in terms of the coefficient of variation of the squared norm identifies the regimes in which ratios of moments suffice (Section~\ref{sec:conc}). In the synthetic experiments, the approximations differ mainly for mixtures normalized as a whole and for laws of low effective dimension (Section~\ref{sec:synth}). Under posterior laws, the estimators differ more for the variance of the cosine than for its mean (Section~\ref{sec:unc}). On incomplete real data we compare both moments with the complete-data cosine (Section~\ref{sec:missing}).

Our contributions are the following.
\begin{itemize}
\item Exact one-dimensional integrals for $\E[x/\|x\|]$ and $\E[xx^\top/\|x\|^2]$ under a Gaussian law with arbitrary, possibly singular, covariance, and their extension to Gaussian mixtures (Theorem~\ref{thm:nu}).
\item The mean and variance of the cosine between independent random vectors, and an expected Gram matrix that is PSD with unit diagonal (Corollary~\ref{cor:cos}).
\item A bound on the error of the ratio-of-moments approximations to both moments in terms of the coefficient of variation of the squared norm (Proposition~\ref{prop:conc}).
\item A quadrature with an adaptive window, and experiments that separate fidelity to the model expectation from prediction of the realized cosine, including an external check of the predicted variance on incomplete data.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{External check of the variance.} Under the fitted law, $\tr(G_iG_j)-\mu_{ij}^2$ predicts the variance of the complete-data cosine $y_{ij}$, which is not drawn from that law. We evaluate it on the pairs with at least one incomplete record. Table~\ref{tab:extvar} reports the ratio of the mean squared error to the mean predicted variance (1 when the predicted scale matches the observed errors), the coverage of the nominal 90\% normal interval, and the Brier score of the predicted probability that $y_{ij}$ exceeds its 90\% quantile under a normal approximation. \EMKcos\ and PN-Taylor understate the observed squared error by 28\% on average (ratio 1.28, coverage 0.88), which is consistent with the fitted law omitting the estimation error of the mixture. For the exceedance probability, \EMKcos\ has a lower Brier score than both moment ratios on all eight representations (0.055 against 0.066--0.068 on average) and than the indicator that its own mean exceeds the threshold (0.073).
